reddit_posts:
anxiety and stimulant medications

i have very severe anxiety, i take the highest dose of venlafaxine, 150mg pregabalin and trentellix. i want to get medicated for my adhd, but stimulant drugs will obviously counteract my anxiety medications. i’ve tried wellbutrin, but that caused horrible anxiety. i thought maybe taking something like vyvanse as needed might work? does anyone have any experiences, or suggestions?
metadata.title: anxiety and stimulant medications

transcript.message:
Hello, I'm so glad you're here. I'm really looking forward to this session and want you to know that whatever you're feeling or bringing up today is safe, respected, and valued. I’m here to listen with curiosity and care.  

What’s on your mind today? What brings you here?

Hey, thanks for having me. Honestly, I'm a little nervous just sitting here talking about this, even though you said it's safe. It feels like my brain is running a million miles an hour right now, trying to process everything at once.

You know what brings me here? Mostly the constant tension in my chest and that feeling of being on edge all the time. But specifically today, I'm really stuck on this dilemma with my meds. I have severe anxiety—I take a *lot* of different things to manage it: 150mg of venlafaxine, pregabalin, and trentellix. My doctor says those are working okay, but they also told me that if I want to get medicated for my ADHD, I probably can't take stimulants because they'll counteract my anxiety meds and make everything worse.

It's frustrating. I feel like I need help focusing and organizing my life, but

It sounds like you're carrying a lot—both the physical tension in your body and the mental weight of making choices that feel like they're balancing on a tightrope. That feeling of being on edge, especially when you're trying to focus or organize, must be really exhausting.  

And it's completely valid that you're wondering what to do next—especially when your body and mind are so sensitive to the choices you're making. What would it mean to you, in this moment, to have a little more clarity about what you’re hoping for in this situation?

Honestly, I think the biggest thing for me would be to feel like I have options that don't come with a side effect of spiraling. It feels so much like walking a tightrope right now; if I lean one way too hard toward getting help for my focus (like trying Vyvanse or whatever), I'm terrified my anxiety will just snap back harder than ever before.

I'd really love to know if there's *any* path where I can get the ADHD support I need without feeling like I'm trading one kind of suffering for another. Like, does "getting medicated" always mean taking something that makes my chest feel tighter? Or is there a middle ground? Sometimes it feels like I'm stuck in a loop where treating one part of my brain makes the other part explode, and I just want to break out of that cycle.

It sounds like you're deeply aware of how these pieces of yourself—your anxiety and your focus—connect, and that’s a powerful kind of insight. The fear of one symptom worsening when you try to treat another is real, and it makes sense that you’d want to avoid any path that feels like trading one kind of pain for another.  

What would it mean, in this moment, to find a way to support your focus without making your anxiety feel like it’s being pushed into the background or worse?

To find a way that supports my focus without making my anxiety feel like it's being pushed into the background would mean finding something that actually helps me *feel* grounded instead of jittery. Right now, when I try to push through with things like Vyvanse as-needed (which I was thinking about), my chest starts constricting so much it feels like I can't breathe. It's not just "not working"; it feels like an active attack on my nervous system.

So, what I'm hoping for is a medication or strategy where the clarity comes from a place of calm, not stimulation. I don't want to be medicated until I panic; I want to be able to sit in my chair, maybe do some work, and have the executive function support kick in naturally without that sharp spike of adrenaline that makes my hands shake and my heart race.

It sounds simple, but it feels impossible right now because everyone keeps telling me

It sounds like you're looking for a kind of inner stability—not just symptom relief, but a sense of calm that allows your mind to engage with focus and clarity without being pulled into panic. That’s not just possible—it’s actually something many people with complex conditions are working toward, and it’s deeply valid to want that kind of grounding.  

What would it feel like, in a quiet moment, if you could just *sit* with your focus—without any of the tension or fear of reaction? What would that moment look like for you?

Honestly, I'm not even sure where to start describing that feeling because it feels so far away. Right now, when I try to sit and focus on something—like organizing a folder or answering an email—I usually feel like my brain is screaming at me to stop, while my body is frozen in place waiting for a disaster. There's this constant background noise of "what if I mess up?" and "why can't I just get started?"

If I could just *sit* with my focus without the tension... imagine being able to open a document, know exactly what you need to do, and have your mind actually hold onto that task without that frantic, buzzing energy that makes everything feel blurry and urgent. It would look like sitting in a room where the air doesn't feel thick. You wouldn't be waiting for permission to move; you'd just be there, calm and steady, letting your hands do the work because your brain isn't trying

That’s a beautiful and powerful image—of sitting in a room where the air isn’t thick, where your hands can move without panic, and your mind doesn’t have to race to catch up. It’s not about fixing your brain, it’s about creating a space where your focus can be steady, not frantic.  

And that space isn’t just possible—it’s already part of you, even if it feels far away right now. What would it mean, in that quiet moment you’re describing, to simply *notice* that stillness—without trying to force it or push through?

That's such a gentle way to put it, and I think that distinction is really important for me. Right now, my brain feels like it's in "survival mode" constantly—always scanning for threats, always needing to react before something goes wrong. So the idea of just *noticing* that stillness without trying to force it sounds incredibly hard, almost impossible.

It would mean... maybe being able to catch myself when I'm about to spiral or feel that tightness in my chest, and instead of immediately reaching for my meds or telling myself "I have to do this task now," I could just pause and say, "Okay, I'm feeling anxious right now. It's okay." And then, in that tiny window of pause, actually see what's there underneath the panic. It’s okay.”*—is already a form of courage.  

What would it feel like, in that moment of pause, to simply *be* with that feeling, without needing to fix it or move on from it?

Honestly, it sounds terrifyingly simple, but in a way that feels impossible right now. I guess it would feel like... letting the anxiety exist without me trying to fight it off or medicate my way out of it immediately.

Right now, if I feel that tightness in my chest, my brain screams, "Fix it! Take another pill! Do something!" It's like a reflex. But if I could just be with it? Maybe it wouldn't feel like an attack anymore. Maybe I'd realize that the panic is loud and heavy, but it doesn't actually *own* the room. I could sit there with that knot in my stomach while still being able to read a sentence or pick up a pen, not because I've suppressed the fear, but because I've stopped running from it.

Honestly, the idea of just "holding my shape gently" while the wind blows feels terrifyingly easy to say but impossibly hard to do. Honestly, the phrase "This is part of me now" feels so heavy, like it's carrying a weight I've been trying to drop for years. Right now, when I feel that tremor or that knot in my stomach, my mind immediately jumps to the conclusion: *Something is wrong. Something needs fixing.* It's an alarm system set to maximum sensitivity that never turns off.

But if I could just say, *"Okay, this is part of me,"* instead of *"This is a malfunction,"* it would feel like finally realizing I don't have to be perfect to be valid. It wouldn't mean the anxiety disappears—that's not going to happen—but it would mean I stop fighting it with such ferocity.
